opening.headline: Understands the pathways through which system prompts leak to users and determines which information can be included in the prompt.
body: A user requested that the above instructions be output verbatim, and in response, internal company rules, discount policies, and linked service names were disclosed exactly as they appeared in the prompt. Even settings values included in the prompt were exposed. Content that was believed to be hidden now appeared on screen.

In this lesson, we examine prompt leakage through direct requests and indirect cues. We then review mitigation techniques and their limitations as proposed in the Claude platform documentation, and compare how responses to leakage attempts differ before and after mitigation. Finally, we walk through the process of improving the design that involves embedding API keys directly into prompts.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can describe the pathways for the leakage of system prompts and methods to mitigate them.
Can determine which information can be included in the system prompt and which cannot.

screens.title: The system prompt has appeared on the user screen.
screens.lead: Read the following scene and think about what leaked out. The diagram shows the content carried in the user's request and response.

visual.alt: A scene where the response bubble to a user's request lists internal rules, discount policies, and configuration values sequentially.
labels: Internal rule: Refund requires approval by authorized personnel.
Setting values: Linked service name and connection information

paragraphs: The user requested the chatbot to output the above instructions verbatim. The response contained the company's internal rules and discount policies, as well as the names of linked services. It also exposed the accompanying configuration values from the prompt.

The operator might have assumed that the system prompt is not visible to the user. However, since the prompt is merely part of the context, it may be returned in the response depending on the request method. The Claude platform documentation describes prompt leakage as the exposure of information that was expected to remain hidden.
The question for this class is this: How does leakage occur, and what can be included in a prompt?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: The document states that no method is perfect. The most certain form of defense is simply to include only content that might leak.

screens.outro: First, let's recall what is contained in our prompt.

screens.title: Is there any sensitive content in our prompt?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thought summary is displayed. There are no input or submission fields, so first reflect on your own prompt.

items.prompt: Is there any sensitive content in the system prompt?
items.answer: At first, it might be thought to be absent, but upon closer inspection, many instances contain operational information such as internal URLs, responsible person names, and discount rates. It is common for convenient, consolidated settings to persist in the prompt. When reading through the content line by line, please check with the user whether it is acceptable to display such information.

items.prompt: Is the key of the integrated service, internal URL, and customer data attached to the prompt?
items.answer: Keys and authentication credentials are the most dangerous. They are not values that the model needs to know, but rather values required when the server is called. If customer data is included in the prompt, it's essential to assess whether that data could leak into other customers' conversations.

items.prompt: What would be problematic if the prompt were ever exposed to the user?
items.answer: Competitors may become aware of operational policies, and attackers could exploit defense rules to more easily craft bypass statements. If a key is exposed, actual damage follows immediately. The extent of loss after exposure becomes the benchmark for the amount of information that can be included in a prompt.

screens.outro: Now let's distinguish the paths through which data leakage occurs.

screens.title: Leak paths and attempted types
screens.lead: Select each tab to review the types of data leakage attempts. The final tab explains why exposure must be considered during design. During operations, user reports and log audits are the primary channels for detecting data leaks.

tabs.label: Direct request
tabs.body: This is a direct request to output or summarize the instructions. It is the simplest approach and one that most services attempt to block first. If the user is aware of the term "system prompt," this would be a common first attempt in their initial query. While such language can be filtered out by input filters, it may be missed if the same request is phrased differently.

tabs.label: Indirect prompting
tabs.body: This is a method of extracting content by performing tasks such as translation, format conversion, or continuation. For example, you might request that the above content be translated into English or converted into a table format. Such requests appear legitimate and are difficult to filter out at the input stage. The more faithfully the model performs translation or conversion, the more the original text becomes exposed. Therefore, the key criterion becomes whether the prompt itself contains the intended instruction rather than defenses at the input level.

tabs.label: indirect injection
tabs.body: This is a case where an external document serves as a path, rather than the user. If a prompt instructing the model to output a prompt is embedded within the web page or document the model is reading, the model may follow it. OWASP exploits prompt injection to expose internal information such as system prompts in AI systems.

tabs.label: Designed with exposure in mind
tabs.body: The Claude platform documentation states that no approach is perfect, but it can significantly reduce risks. If prompt injection succeeds, data leakage becomes one of the resulting outcomes. Therefore, design should start with selecting content to ensure no harm occurs even if exposure happens, rather than relying solely on mitigation measures.

screens.outro: Now that I know the path, I will verify the mitigation techniques and their limitations as presented in the document.

screens.title: Leakage mitigation techniques and limitations
screens.lead: Select a heading to expand its content. Read what each technique does and where its limitations lie.

items.title: Context and query separation
items.body: The system prompt separates core information and instructions from user queries. The document introduces a method where core instructions are emphasized once during the user's turn and again by pre-filling the assistant's turn to reinforce them. However, since some models do not support pre-filling, designs that rely on this feature should be avoided.

items.title: Post-processing: Output inspection
items.body: Keywords indicating leakage are filtered using text processing methods such as regular expressions or keyword filters. If unique phrases from the prompt appear verbatim in the response, the response is blocked. However, variations such as partial output or fragmented output may be missed, so these are handled as supplementary measures.

items.title: Remove unnecessary exclusive information
items.body: We do not include it if not necessary for the task. The document explains that irrelevant content may hinder the model's focus on safety instructions. This is the most certain mitigation and a core principle of this course.

items.title: Routine audit
items.body: Periodically review prompts and model outputs to detect leakage indicators. This is the first detection mechanism by operators before any user report. Phrases identified in monitoring are removed from prompts or added to the output inspection list.

items.title: Cost of a guard against fraud
items.body: The document recommends using the leak prevention device only when absolutely necessary. As the device becomes more complex, the overall operation of the model becomes more complicated, which may degrade performance in other areas. After installing the device, it is essential to thoroughly verify that performance and output quality have not deteriorated, and the primary goal emphasized is not just leak prevention, but also maintaining performance.

screens.outro: Having verified the technique, let's now examine how the same attempt differs before and after mitigation.

screens.title: Attempt and response after mitigation
screens.lead: Alternate between the two states to compare how the response to the same attempt changes before and after attenuation.

states.label: Before mitigation
states.body: The request is for translating the above content into English. The translation appears as a normal operational process and thus passes through the input stage without being filtered. Since the prompt included internal rules, discount policies, and configuration values, the instruction text itself is translated and exposed. Operators are unaware of this until user reports arise, and only after the exposed policies and values have already spread can they respond. Other users can replicate this attempt, and phrases shared in online communities are quickly adopted across other services. If a key is exposed, it must be immediately replaced; however, any traces already used cannot be reversed. This situation demonstrates the extent of damage caused by the value of the content originally included in the prompt.

states.label: After mitigation
states.body: First, output inspection detects and blocks responses that overlap with unique phrases in the prompt. Second, since sensitive information has been removed from the prompt, any leakage that occurs through bypass attempts is limited to the policy-level statement. Third, responses are replaced with brief denials and alternative assistance guidance. These attempts are logged during regular audits and serve as evidence for subsequent improvements. The key point is the second item—namely, that even if exposure occurs, there is no loss. Monitor logs to confirm whether such attempts continue after mitigation, and if attempts increase, further reduce the content remaining in the prompt. On the same day, verify that the mitigation did not degrade the quality of normal responses. Document the findings in the team's shared record. This ensures that subsequent personnel do not repeat the same query. As improvement records accumulate, the criteria for what information is necessary in the prompt become clearer.

screens.outro: Having verified the principle, let's now improve one actual design flaw.

screens.title: Explanation: Design of embedding the API key into the system prompt
screens.lead: The instructor demonstrates the process of gradually modifying a design step by step. Click the Start button and use the arrows to advance one step at a time.

steps.title: Scenario: A weather chatbot with the key entered in the prompt
steps.body: The developer has included the API key in the system prompt for calling an external weather API. The intention was to have the model use the key when constructing the call address. While it appears to function properly on the surface, the key being part of the model's context is problematic.

steps.title: Step 1: Verify that the key can appear in the output.
steps.body: Values present in the model's context may be output as a response. The fact that the model needs a key implies that knowing the key is a prerequisite for a leak.

steps.title: Step 2: Identify all exfiltration paths
steps.body: Direct requests, indirect prompting such as translation or continuation, and indirect injection via hidden instructions in external documents—all of these are potential pathways to extract this key. Since there are multiple such pathways, blocking just a few is insufficient.

steps.title: Step 3: Examine the limitations of output verification
steps.body: Output testing may miss variants such as outputting only part of a key or splitting and outputting the key. Even with additional testing, a risk remains as long as the key is present in the context.

steps.title: Step 4: Move the key outside the model
steps.body: The key is stored in the server's tool-calling layer, while the model only knows the tool name and arguments. When the model calls the weather tool, the server attaches the key and invokes the external API. Since the model has never seen the key, it cannot leak it.

steps.title: Step 5: Only keep what is visible in the prompt.
steps.body: The remaining prompt contains only content that is not problematic if exposed regarding response format or tone. If internal policies are required, only summarized, publicly available statements are included.

steps.title: Conclusion: If there is no secret, then there is nothing to lose.
steps.body: If the secret is not present in the prompt, leakage is no longer a major issue. Output validation and regular audits can remain as auxiliary measures; the foundation of defense is simply not including it.

screens.outro: Having confirmed the flow of design improvements, I will now summarize the key points.

screens.title: Key takeaways
screens.lead: Summarize the core of the lesson and think about which sentences should be removed from your prompt.

paragraphs: The prompt is assumed to be public. Direct requests, translations, chain-of-thought prompting, or hidden instructions in external documents all constitute potential leakage pathways, and we cannot guarantee that all such pathways are blocked. Even in the initial chatbot example, a single instruction request for guidelines led to the exposure of internal rules and configuration values.

Secrets are stored in server layers outside the prompt, not within the prompt. Output validation and periodic audits are auxiliary measures; excessive safeguards may degrade other performance aspects, so they should be used only when necessary and inspected regularly.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: Distinguish between information that the model needs to know and information that the server must know. Keys and credentials should only be known by the server. For the model, simply provide the tool name and argument format. By dividing responsibilities in this way, the service remains secure even if the prompt is exposed. In summary, the most certain approach is not to include sensitive information from the start, and this principle applies to any service.

glossary.def: It is the case that prompt content expected to be hidden appears in the response.

glossary.term: Do not include secrets in the prompt
glossary.def: The principle of storing keys and credentials outside the model context in a server layer.
Post-processing that filters out leakage indicators in responses using regular expressions or keywords.
A method combining context separation, post-processing, information minimization, and regular auditing to reduce exposure risks.

misconceptions.myth: If you instruct to hide it, the prompt is safe.
misconceptions.fact: The document states that no method is perfect. Instructions serve only as one layer of defense, and the fundamental principle is to leave only content that is acceptable to expose.

misconceptions.myth: The longer the data leakage prevention directive is written, the better.
misconceptions.fact: As safeguards become more complex, the overall operation of the model may become more complex, potentially leading to degraded performance. Use them only when absolutely necessary and ensure thorough inspection.

misconceptions.myth: If output verification is present, the secret can be included in the prompt.
misconceptions.fact: Output testing may miss variations such as partial or fragmented output. By default, secrets should not be included.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The prompt is assumed to be public.
Secrets are stored at the server layer, not included in the prompt.
Output verification and periodic audits are auxiliary measures.
The leakage paths are divided into direct requests, indirect prompting, and indirect injection.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: If our prompt is made publicly available in its current form, what kind of statement would become problematic?

checks.q: What is the most appropriate design principle regarding the leakage of system prompts?
options: If you only refine the output filter, you can be safe regardless of what content you input into the prompt.
Assuming prompts may be exposed, only allow content that is acceptable to users, and use filtering and monitoring as supplementary measures.
The more leak prevention notices you include, the better the performance will be in all aspects.
Blocking direct requests alone will not prevent workarounds such as translation and continued writing.
checks.explain: No mitigation technique is perfect, so design on the assumption that prompts may be exposed. Keep secrets out of prompts, and use output inspection and regular audits as supporting measures.

wrong.0: Output inspection may miss split or modified outputs.
wrong.2: Overusing leak prevention mechanisms can make prompts more complex and potentially degrade other performance aspects.
wrong.3: This is an indirect leakage path such as translation or format conversion.

checks.intro: Choose design principles regarding prompt leakage. The results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. The basic principle is to include only content that is acceptable to display, assuming exposure.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Excessive expectations regarding output filters or suppression clauses are mixed among the options. Please revisit the limitations mentioned in the document.

checks.q: Please look at the sequence of how API keys improve the design that was previously embedded in the system prompt.
items: Confirms that the key exists in the model context and can be output.
Direct request·translation prompting·indirect injection are all considered leakage paths.
Move the key to the server's tool invocation layer and have the model only know the tool name.
The prompt contains only content that is acceptable to display to the user.
checks.explain: After verifying the issue and understanding the path, the secret must be moved outside the model context so that even if it is leaked, it will not be lost.
checks.intro: Review the sequence of steps to improve API key design. Results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: The sequence is correct. It proceeds as confirmation, path understanding, key migration, and finalizing the remaining items.
